cells.tense: Right here, with the pen, this has run its course and you are letting it close.
cells.act: trade one thing for one thing, and keep no score
cells.ask: Pick an exchange you're in the middle of with someone. Make it a straight swap — what you give matched by what you get — and keep no tally of who owes whom after.
cells.core:
The ending and the push run on the same fairness here: you hand back what this was owed, the goal gets clear road, and the exchange keeps moving without a ledger in your hands. That is how it stays clean. Something that lived gets set down, whoever was in it gets what their part earned, and the road toward what's next opens. Nobody has to come up short for the closing to happen. Fairness and finishing are one motion, and both keep moving.
There's a person or a piece you'd wait on if you could. Settle that part first — take your half out, pay what your share owes, hand theirs back to them. Some of what you're moving toward gets asked about before the clearing finishes, and you'll answer cleaner with the books straight. Let the first settlement show you what the movement feels like when nothing is outstanding. What it costs to keep an exchange even, you already pay gladly.
cells.sheetLine: You let a thing finish and keep the road clear after it.
cells.verb: let what is finished finish and turn the cleared ground toward the goal
cells.place: on the road toward the thing you are after, between one work and the next

cells.tense: You are already braced for the next ending before this one has had its life.
cells.act: feel it alongside them and keep your own side
cells.ask: Choose someone with a stake in whether this survives. Say what the ending looks like from where you stand, then stop talking and let their whole week reach you, not just the part about this.
cells.core:
You can feel a thing ending before it has finished, and you've started clearing ground before the actual close. Your year reads as a string of fresh starts, each one up fast, each one already braced for the next break. From outside it looks like freedom. From inside it's the fear of what happens if something runs all the way to its natural end around you. Nothing gets to live long enough to prove it's safe.
Not every ending needs clearing yet. Some still have their own length to run. Sit with one person who's in this with you, without trying to fix what they feel, and stay in contact while it's hard — you keep your own side, they keep theirs, and you're still there through the middle. That last part hasn't happened yet, and it's the one that would tell you whether the ending you keep reaching for is real.

cells.tense: You are still standing where this went through a long while back.
cells.ask: Take one step toward what you actually want — an email, a call, a single sentence sent — and do it before you feel like it, not after.
cells.core:
You're pointed at something, and you aren't arriving. Something already closed, and part of you still keeps the shape it had: the same course, the same losses, and the name you have for it is staying true. Nothing new gets a beginning because the old thing hasn't been released. Loyalty to what's over can pass for patience, and it isn't. It's the same movement, stalled, one street back.
Let the feeling pull, then move with it. Something in you is already heading somewhere, even if you won't give it that name. Send the smallest next piece today — a sentence, a call — before you're ready, because the readiness may not show up first. The step is what carries you through. You don't have to see the destination from where you're standing. You just have to be further than this morning.

cells.tense: Something is already over, and you are steering the whole goal around it unnamed.
cells.act: give the mess a shape it can be carried in
cells.ask: Take the tangled part of this you don't look at much. Put it into one shape on paper — what's in it, what's closed, what's still open, a line each — then read it once.
cells.core:
You keep steering around something this goal already ended, and you haven't named it. The direction is measured against a thing that isn't there anymore, and the gap doesn't show. It stays out of view because naming it would mean a chapter that closes, and the structure you run on doesn't have that page yet. Everything else in the push gets a plan.
Put a shape around the mess and look at it once. One page: what's in it, what's over, what's still live, a line each. Not a decision, not the ending — just the thing made small enough to carry. The act is the structure itself, not the answer it produces. What you're doing is giving the direction somewhere to stand, so the goal can run from what's actually present instead of from something you haven't looked at. You don't have to end it to see it plainly. Seeing it is the whole ask.
cells.sheetLine: The goal is steered around something already over.

attempts.check: The draft I'd flag: I catch myself claiming this person ends things well here — 'you let things end when they're done and move on toward the goal.' The record gives only that endings flow from felt necessity, not that they're honored on time or aimed at the goal. The reader could say 'no — I end things, but never when they're finished, and often not the right ones.' The ask survives a wrong read because backing two people even when you're wrong is simply steadying, not a loss. The sentence that serves me more than them is any variation on 'you know which things are already over' — that flatters the writer's neatness and pins a universal on their life.
